requested.title: Shell expansion bypasses all protected Git-command checks

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: The finding was valid in the committed baseline: its own former header explicitly stated that `g=git; $g reset --hard` passed, because `gitInvocation()` only recognized literal `git` tokens. The current working tree patches that boundary in `command-guard.ts`: tokenization records unescaped shell expansions and glob syntax, and `checkSegment()` rejects an indirect executable before attempting Git recognition. It also rejects expansion/glob use in Git globals and subcommands, and in arguments for policy-bearing commands including `config`, `commit`, `checkout`, `stash`, `clean`, and `switch`. Active `$()` and backtick substitutions are recursively inspected, while `eval`, `source`, `.`, and related evaluators are denied; this prevents the shell from resolving an unchecked Git invocation after authorization. The effective execution path is guarded: the OpenCode supervisor passes every non-local `bash` permission through `decidePermission()`, which calls `checkCommand()` before replying `once`; `run_background` independently calls the same guard. Local OpenCode runs currently disable the `bash` capability altogether, so the claimed local shell route is not available through that permission path. The uncommitted regression tests directly cover variable-expanded, command-substituted, quoted, glob-derived, wrapper-derived, and local-scope `git push`, destructive Git, and dangerous `git config` cases. I did not execute tests because this review is restricted to static analysis, but the source-level mitigation matches the stated bypass and is wired into the authorization points.
